q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE policy associated with the shift toward free markets in the late twentieth century.
parts.b: Explain ONE reason why communist command economies collapsed or were reformed at the end of the twentieth century, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE difference between China's economic reforms and Russia's economic reforms after the Cold War.

sample_answers.a: Governments privatized state-owned industries, deregulated markets, cut taxes, and opened economies to foreign trade and investment — as in Thatcher's Britain, Reagan's America, and Deng's China.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, command economies could not match the productivity and innovation of market systems; chronic shortages, technological backwardness, and falling living standards delegitimized communist rule and forced reform or collapse.
sample_answers.c: China reformed gradually under continued Communist Party control, maintaining political authority while introducing markets; Russia attempted rapid 'shock therapy' privatization amid political chaos, producing economic collapse and oligarchic corruption.

q1.stimulus:
Historians describe the late twentieth century as the age of the market's triumph. From the late 1970s onward, leaders across the political spectrum — Deng Xiaoping in China, Margaret Thatcher in Britain, Ronald Reagan in the United States — dismantled controls, privatized state industries, and opened their economies to global competition. The collapse of the Soviet bloc between 1989 and 1991 seemed to confirm the verdict: command economies, for all their early achievements in industrialization, could not sustain innovation or satisfy consumer desires, while market systems, for all their inequalities, generated wealth and adapted to change. Yet historians also note the costs: deindustrialization devastated communities, inequality soared, and the market's triumph left many feeling that democracy itself had been subordinated to the demands of capital.
—Historian's account of free-market reforms in the period c. 1900–present

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE claim Reagan makes about the role of government in the economy.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which Reagan's policies put this claim into practice.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why Reagan's critique of government resonated with voters in 1980.

sample_answers.a: Reagan claims that government is not the solution to economic problems but the problem itself — that excessive taxation, regulation, and spending stifle the productive energy of the American people.
sample_answers.b: His administration cut income taxes, deregulated industries (such as airlines and banking), and sought to reduce domestic spending, shifting resources and initiative from the public sector to private enterprise.
sample_answers.c: After the stagflation, energy crises, and perceived failures of the 1970s, many voters blamed government intervention for economic misery and were receptive to the argument that freeing markets would restore prosperity.

q2.stimulus:
In this present crisis, government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem. From time to time we've been tempted to believe that society has become too complex to be managed by self-rule, that government by an elite group is superior to government for, by, and of the people. But if no one among us is capable of governing himself, then who among us has the capacity to govern someone else?
—President Ronald Reagan, Inaugural Address, 20 January 1981

q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE feature of the photograph that symbolizes the end of communist rule in Eastern Europe.
parts.b: Explain ONE way in which the fall of the Berlin Wall reflected the failure of command economies.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which the end of the Cold War accelerated the spread of free-market policies.

sample_answers.a: East Germans climbing and celebrating atop the Wall — the hated barrier that had imprisoned them — visually captures the popular rejection of communist rule and the triumph of the desire for freedom.
sample_answers.b: East Germany's collapse showed that even the most successful communist economy could not provide the prosperity and consumer goods its citizens saw in the West; the Wall fell because the system behind it had lost economic and moral credibility.
sample_answers.c: With the Soviet model discredited, Western advisers and institutions (the IMF, World Bank) pressed former communist states to privatize, deregulate, and open markets rapidly, presenting free-market capitalism as the only viable path.

q3.stimulus: The photograph shows the Berlin Wall at the Brandenburg Gate after its fall in November 1989, with East and West Berliners celebrating together atop the barrier that had divided the city since 1961. The Wall's collapse — the result of mass protests and the East German government's loss of control — became the defining image of communism's fall in Eastern Europe and the symbolic end of the Cold War division of the continent.
